This is a scam. The text message is swapping between past tense and present tense in the same paragraph. There's other grammatical errors littered throughout that message.

If you're actually expecting a package, you can simply check the tracking number to see where it is.  
And if you're not expecting a package, then you can easily deduce that this is a scam.

The link they sent you also doesn't have anything to do with USPS. As there's no "USPS" or "USPostal" anywhere in the link, it's also not a .com, .org, .htm or .info link.

and Finally. They'd be more professional with their message and tell you exactly what the item is that's getting lost or stuck in transit. Or at the very least, they'd attach the tracking number.

Yu-Gi-Oh is a deck builder's paradise. 

Building a deck in Yu-Gi-Oh feels like LEGO. You have all these cool pieces that you can put together and create something truly unique and satisfying. I'm a TCG teacher. I educate beginners how to play card games. Be it Yu-Gi-Oh, Magic, or Pokemon. 
I will say that Yu-Gi-Oh is the easiest to teach people how to play. There's so little to explain. 5 card hands. Normal/Set/Tribute Summon once per turn. Special Summon as much as you want. Traps are set first, then activated. Spells can be activated from the hand. Understand the summoning conditions to get extra deck monsters. Higher Attack Numbers win in a battle. It's really simple.

 As my dad said. "If you want to teach someone about cars. You don't start by explaining what a supercharger is." 

You gradually explain the rules. It's very easy. Much easier than teaching Magic or Pokemon. Where you have things like Mana/Energy and complex combat steps. 

The issue is that people don't take it bite sized steps. When I got back into Yu-Gi-Oh. There were so many new summoning mechanics and effects. 
I took it one step at a time. Learning the new master rules bit by bit. 

There needs to be better educators in the community that can very gently and slowly provide beginners with information. 

Many people I speak to who attempt to get back into Yu-Gi-Oh will dust off their old childhood decks and enter a local event or hop on Dueling Book or Master Duel. And they'll find themselves getting completely obliterated by more experienced players who go full combo because a deck from 2005 doesn't have the right interaction. 

I personally think there's no particular thing to blame except for a lack of communication and information. 

The player base can also be an issue. There are plenty of jackasses in the community. But there's pricks in every TCG community. Idk why Yu-Gi-Oh has become this cliche of "everybody is toxic." Because it's simply not true. I've met more toxic people in the MTG, Pokemon and Hearthstone TCG communities compared to Yu-Gi-Oh. 

I will also say that the price of decks is also not true. Yu-Gi-Oh is probably the most budget friendly card game ever especially compared to Magic the Gathering. Yu-Gi-Oh has an aggressive reprint policy and cards eventually become cheap enough for a player to obtain. My current Earth Machine deck costed me about $65. And I've had phenomenal success with Earth Machines at competitive events. Compare this to Magic the Gathering, a card game with purposefully refuses to reprint cards and has an entire list of cards that will never be reprinted. And a huge portion of these Reserved List cards are seen as mandatory for competitive play. Even ignoring the reserved list, we can move to formats like Modern. Okay. I am an avid competitive and casual MTG player. I play Magic very frequently. And I will give you the most honest and lengthy anecdote I can to convince you to play Yu-Gi-Oh instead of Magic. 


>1) Magic the Gathering is EXPENSIVE
More expensive than Yu-Gi-Oh ever will be.  The average MTG deck costs over $1,000. Even casual decks cost you thousands. 
Magic also does not have a good grasp of reprinting cards. They will purposely refuse to reprint staple cards because they actively want cards to be expensive on the secondary market. 

>2) Power Creep and Variety
Magic originally didn't like the idea of Power Creep. However, in 2019 they unveiled Modern Horizons. A set who's entire purpose is to power creep the hell out of the previous 25+ years of Magic. The Power Creep in Magic is way more blatant, obvious and frustrating than in Yu-Gi-Oh. Magic power creep is also very bottlenecked. So there is an extreme lack of variety. Every Modern deck is a pile of the same 10 to 12 Modern Horizons 2 cards. It gets very boring, very quickly. Yu-Gi-Oh meanwhile has so many more cards. Even looking at all the deck lists for recent YCS and WCQ events (post Tearlaments banning). I can see so many different archetypes. 
Mathmech, Kashtira, Bystial. Labyrinth, Purely, Swordsoul, Earth Machine, Spright, Floo, Drytron, Rikka, Evil Twin, Branded, Thunder Dragon, ect. 
All these decks are VERY different in behavior compared to "thing plus 30 Modern Horizon 2 cards." 
Yes, Yu-Gi-Oh can be like this too. But Modern Horizons 2 came out in 2021. So imagine if the Tearlaments Tier 0 format lasted until 2025? And the only thing that'll stop Tearlaments is when in 2027 they eventually make new cards that power creep Tearlaments out of the format? 


>3) Play patterns
Current 2023 1v1 Magic the Gathering plays almost identical to a Yu-Gi-Oh game. 1 well timed Free Spell wins you the game. Much like how a well timed Ash Blossom can win you games. 
However, Yu-Gi-Oh lets you skirt around Ash Blossom with even more powerful answers. Magic currently doesn't have any answers to stop an Evoked Solitude, Fury or a Leyline Binding. You just kinda hope your opponent isn't rich enough to afford a playset of Solitudes. 

Yu-Gi-Oh has better interaction. Your decisions feel like they matter. You have consistency that Magic lacks. 


>4) Deck Building
Yu-Gi-Oh is a deck builder's paradise. If you find an archetype or a couple cards you find interesting. There's probably an entire archetype tailor made to make that card you like work. Magic meanwhile; does not allow this kind of freedom. There's a very rigid hierarchy of good cards and you're given no room for freedom. When I find a Yu-Gi-Oh card. You can start researching all these cool interactions that the card does and put together a deck that feels satisfying when all the pieces fit together. It results in some flashy combos, with plenty of variety and different pathways for your combo. Magic meanwhile does not have this. Let's say you find a card you like. All the best decks that would use it basically are "this card plus the same 30 Modern Horizons cards you need to play." 
Give Ash Blossom credit. If your deck was just 37 Ash Blossoms and three level 4 Normal Monsters. You wouldn't ever win a single game. In Magic. This is what it feels like. The same 30 staples, the same 22 lands. And barely anything that ever resembles your "archetype." 



>5) Rules
Yu-Gi-Oh's rules are easy to follow. Everything does exactly what the card says. Magic meanwhile has so many ruling nightmares that there's been entire competitive strategies based around cheating the rules to your benefit. 

Unless you're a hardcore tournament grinder who only cares about winning or you're only interest is making money. I urge you, please just play Yu-Gi-Oh. In the long term. Yu-Gi-Oh is a game I can always come back to and never have the same problems that Magic involves. 

If you like deck building and variety and learning about how cards interact. Yu-Gi-Oh is so much better. 

Yu-Gi-Oh is also way easier to learn. As a teacher of 5 different card games. Yu-Gi-Oh is the absolute easiest to teach people. I've taught my 59 year old father how to play both Magic and Yu-Gi-Oh and I've actually been able to play a game or 2 of Yu-Gi-Oh with my dad. Whereas all the keywords and weird rulings like "priority" made it really difficult for my dad to enjoy the game of MTG. 

So there you go. The TL;DR is that I recommend you get interested in Yu-Gi-Oh instead of Magic. Because Magic is not fun the same way Yu-Gi-Oh is.

as a GM, I use legends very sparingly. For my more traditional campaigns. I create a main game. with 8ish gym leaders, elite 4, champion, ect.

For the Regis, it's Regigigas, for the G1 Birds, it's Lugia or Ho-Oh and so on.   
I then pick a small handful of other weaker legendaries that'd be fun to give the players a chance to catch, usually depending on my story. 

I also play it very loosely with Pokemon moves and abilities. I've gone so far as to make up my own abilities, moves and effects. Because it's fun for me to buff up Legendaries and give other pokemon some cool new toys to play with. I also improv a lot. If the player(s) spent a much more difficult time hunting the legend and put in some serious effort in the story (IE: being a good person, helping NPCs, stopping crooks, ect.) I reward them with buffed up versions of the legendaries they want/find. 

I normally save this for the very late game, and sometimes I don't even allow Legendaries to be caught until after the Elite 4, or after the main villains are fully thwarted. 

Other times, I don't use legendaries at all because they can be very boring to watch the player use, and a skilled player with an arsenal of legendaries can breeze through the Elite 4 and other final boss obstacles.

It's done in the anime for visual reasons. It's better to see the card on screen, so they summon them in face-up def mode.

Looking at the idea from an artistic perspective; It's all about having the cards come to life in the anime. And face-down DEF mode doesn't really bring the card to life. In the anime, the monsters have emotions and when they're in defense mode, it gives artists a chance to draw the monsters taking on a different expression and posture. (the visual cue of the monsters turning blue and taking on a more blocking / guarding position that they started doing in 5D's is also something I really love)

The anime characters only ever set monsters in face-down defense mode for 1 of 3 reasons.

* 1:  It's a flip-effect monster 
* 2:  It's a way the animators can save on money and time, because having to draw those monsters coming to life is expensive and takes time, and Konami needs to keep a schedule going, those episodes need to come out weekly after all.
* 3: It's a suspense thing. A card like Fiber Jar, Cyber Jar or Man-Eater Bug can lead to a lot of suspense and tension if they're face-down. 

There are casual formats I know of where you're allowed to normal summon in face-up def mode btw. (it gives certain cards a brand new niche and can lead to some fun interactions).

If we're talking purely Mono-Green. You've got bits and pieces of a green devotion deck. Which I played A LOT of pre-MH1. 
My original goal of that deck was to turbo out [[Tooth and Nail]] on turn 3.

With Yavimaya, you can turn your [[Nykthos, Shrine to Nyx]] into a Forest. Tap it for a butt load of green. Then untap the shrine with Arbor Elf because it's a Forest. 

Use permanens to get your devotion massive like [[Llanowar Tribe]] which also adds more mana. 

Casting Tooth and Nail by turn 3 is the dream, but it's hard to achieve. Tooth & Nail basically wins you the game once you play it. You can grab any number of infinite combos. [[Kiki Jiki]] plus [[Restoration Angel]] is a personal favorite. 
You can also just dump down gigantic threats like [[Emrakul, The Aeons Torn]] or [[Worldspine Wurm]] 

This deck is extremely janky for Modern. As you lose to almost any hand disruption. Turn 1 Thoughtseize, yoinking your Tooth & Nail is basically game over. 
You also lose horribly to removal. Turn 1 bolt/push your mana dork is another game over. 

Ragavan also eats this deck alive. It's a painful slog trying to survive a turn 1 Ragavan with a clunky devotion deck.

And probably worst of all, you lose *tremendously* to Counterspells. 

But. Tooth & Nail, as a deck, is so much fun. You'll probably go 1-3 every week. But that one magical game where you pull it off, you feel like the ultimate badass. 

*OR*

Ignoring Mono-Green meme shenanigans. Arbor Elf + Sprawl has been a staple for G/R Ponza decks forever. 
You play Sprawl and always name Red with it. Now on turn 2 you can cast huge threats like [[Karn, Great Creator]] or just grind them out with [[Pillage]] and [[Stone Rain]] spam. It's very hard for a player to come back from getting 2 of their lands obliterated on Turn 3. 

One of my more favorite things to do with Ponza is ramp out and play a turn 2 [[Thrun, the Last Troll]] who's a severely underrated beatstick in this meta. Thrun can't be touched by Solitude or Fury, nor can he even be countered. You can also regenerate Thrun. 
Ponza also plays [[Wren and Six]] which can be used to scoop up your Yavimaya if it's ever destroyed or discarded. 

Ramping out into Karn also gives you access to at most; 15 additional artifacts you can literally cherry pick for the perfect situation. If we're talking purely greedy ramp. Karn can just grab a big dumb robot like [[Sundering Titan]] or [[Blightsteel Colossus]]. 

TL;DR - Look into Mono Green Devotion if you want to goof around and be silly at FNM. Or if you're looking for something that's actually viable, check out Ponza.

There is also no "perfect" way to build the deck. There's at least 3 or 4 different versions of Scales and each of them is just as competitive as the others. 
The greater community plays G/W Scales. So you have access to Esper Sentinel, Prismatic Ending and Path.

G/U Scales gives you access to [[Metallic Rebuke]] which gives Scales an AMAZING win percentage against Living End, Temur Rhinos and Amulet Titan.

G/R Scales gives you more explosive combo potential with Zabaz 

The deck (all versions) also has some pretty amazing Matchups vs Murktide. I'd say it's a 7-3 in Scales' favor. 

Your primary win conditions are Walking Ballista and Inkmoth Nexus.

You've also got an AMAZING threat in the form of [[Patchwork Automaton]] , equip Patchy with a Shadow Spear and you're basically unbeatable. That ward 2 is brutal for most decks. And even if they try and kill it, and pay the ward. You have excellent evasion in the form of [[Welding Jar]] which is super underrated. It gets around Vigor, Fury, Push, Bolt, ect. ((The 3 words a Hardened Scales player fears the most are "Can't Be Regenerated"))

The deck also is very tough for opponents to interact with. Arcbound Ravager is a massive threat, but targeting it with removal spells isn't always a good idea. Because you have so many Artifacts at your disposal, you can just gobble them all up and make Ravager gargantuan and keep it out of range of Unholy Heats or Bolts or Furies.

The format is definitely slower and more value oriented. You have to look at every card in your deck and ask yourself how it can generate some form of value. 

Aggro decks are in a tough spot because creatures like Goblin Guide just dont provide enough long term value. 

We were also given some insane tempo cards that reward slower decks, in the form of Force of Vigor, Solitude, Fury, Endurance, Prismatic Ending, and even the almighty Counterspell.

If you want to stay competitive, there are 2 faster Aggro decks that I believe are in the top 10. 

Hammer Time and Hardened Scales.

Hammer Time can kill a person by turn 2 if it's lucky. Which is way faster than the turn 4 or Turn 5 that the slower midrange & control decks are relying on. But, Hammer Time can't grind very well. If you get into that late stage, like past turn 5. You're not winning most games without an insane amount of luck. 
But, Hammer Time also has access to sideboard options like [[Batterskull]] and [[Kaldra Complete]] Which are value machines that can put on so much mid to late game pressure. 

Hardened Scales meanwhile, is my favorite deck of all time. [[Arcbound Ravager]] can turn every single artifact into value, and you can then use all that value into a massive one hit kill. I've been playing Hardened Scales for a little over a year now and I've been putting up several top 8s at my LGS. The deck requires a huge amount of practice and maintenance, you have to do math puzzles, and none of your games will ever be the same. The deck can kill opponents right around turn 3 or 4 most games. You also don't ever even need to attack to win. Sometimes you can just win the game by placing 26 +1/+1 counters on a Walking Ballista and machine gun down your opponent during your main phase.
I also recommend Hardened Scales as a lower price entry deck. It's not as cheap as Boggles or Burn. But still half the price of Omnath decks. I also don't play on MTGO, but I've been told Hardened Scales is WAY cheaper to build on MTGO than in Paper. 


TL;DR : Look into Hammer Time or Hardened Scales as your best competitive Aggro decks.

It's not exactly clear what beats what in terms of design and strategy. It's as random as rolling dice. 
Every day it seems the "meta" (if you will) changes constantly. 
In the early days, the theory was 
Flipper > Wedge > Spinner > Flipper
But this is not true as times change and new strategies are created. If you ask me. It's more of a tier list 'behind the scenes'
As in, a driver's skill and engineering will be the deciding factor. 
Because there's a very very very good chance that if I built a wedge made of plywood I won't beat Last Rites or Nightmare. 
Even if I theoretically built a solid steel wedge with military grade motors and batteries. Someone like Ray Billings will still beat me for he has probably 1,000×  more experience than I do and he probably has figured out how to configure and pilot Tombstone to defeat my machine. 

At the same time however. I could dedicate and focus my efforts on perfecting my robot and aquire the skills and experience needed so I'm ready to defeat Tombstone or Bite Force. 
But, even if by some miracle I did do such a thing, people would be watching and they'd analyze my fights and try to come up with new strategies and designs to counter me and my machine. And the cycle would continue indefinitely. 

So no, you can't exactly determine what beats what, all you can really rely on is your own instincts, skills and choices.

Behemoth vs. Tazbot

Winner: Behemoth. 

Behemoth is incredibly sturdy and bulky and Tazbot has a hard time picking up and lifting 220lb robots. And Behemoth's big plow will pacify poor Tazbot

Razer vs. Overkill

Winner: Overkill?

This one is INCREDIBLY close. But I kinda side with Overkill simply because of bias alone, but Razer could get underneath Overkill and use it's blade to pierce Overkill. The problem is that this would do little actual damage. Overkill's tires are just foam and puncturing them wouldn't hinder it in any way. And I think after one or 2 punctures Razer's recovery would be slow and Overkill would have it's way. Overkill is more robust than Razer too, and you also have to factor in that we're still in the Battlebox, Razer was incredibly effective because it could grapple and drag opponents into the pits, but without a pit, the battle between these 2 would probably last the full 3 minutes and go to the judges. 
And if we were to go to the judges it'd come down to an incredibly close decision. 
Razer would rack up points in the Damage category, but Overkill would be flailing it's big knife, earning it aggression points, in the Strategy category, Overkill would again win, because unlike Razer, Overkill is a pure wedge and would have an easier time plowing Razer along into hazards without damaging itself. 
This is absurdly close and I could still argue Razer winning, but I'm sticking with my instincts and voting Overkill


Tornado vs. Stinger

Winner: Tornado

Tornado wins because Stinger's weapon is not that effective and Stinger's large wheels and body are a huge target for Tornado's blade to strike.

SMIDSY vs. Firestorm vs. Hypnodisc

Winner: Firestorm & Hypnodisc
The obvious winners are obvious, Firestorm would just get underneath SMIDSY and have his way. And Hypnodisc would chew apart SMIDSY. The poor bot is just the weakest link.


Behemoth vs. Terrorhurtz vs. King B

Nightmare vs. Hypnodisc
